questions.q: Aldehydes and ketones react with HCN by:
questions.solution:
**Nucleophilic addition.** The carbonyl carbon is $\delta+$ because oxygen is far more electronegative, so it attracts nucleophiles.

$\text{CN}^{-}$ attacks it, the $\pi$ electrons move onto the oxygen, and protonation gives the cyanohydrin.

questions.q: Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with:
questions.solution:
Only **aldehydes** reduce the silver(I) complex to metallic silver.

Oxidising a ketone would require breaking a carbon-carbon bond, which Tollens' cannot do. It is the standard distinction between the two.

questions.q: The triiodomethane (iodoform) test is positive for:
questions.solution:
A yellow precipitate of $\text{CHI}_{3}$ forms from anything containing a $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}-$ group, or a $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)}-$ group that is oxidised to one in the conditions.

So ethanal and propanone give it; propanal does not. It is a test for a **fragment**, not a functional group, which is what makes it so useful in structure determination.
options: methyl ketones and methyl secondary alcohols

questions.q: Carboxylic acids are more acidic than alcohols because:
questions.solution:
The carboxylate ion's negative charge is **delocalised over two equivalent oxygen atoms**, which stabilises it enormously.

An alkoxide has no such delocalisation, so the alcohol holds its proton far more tightly. $\text{p}K_{a}$: about $4.8$ against $16$.
options: the carboxylate ion is stabilised by delocalisation

questions.q: An ester is formed from a carboxylic acid and:
questions.solution:
$\text{RCOOH} + \text{R}'\text{OH} \rightleftharpoons \text{RCOOR}' + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, with concentrated sulphuric acid as catalyst.

The reaction is **reversible**, so the yield is improved by removing the water or using an excess of one reagent.

questions.q: Find the molar mass of propanone, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{3}$, in g/mol.
How many aldehyde and ketone isomers together does $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}$ have (open chain)?
How many moles of NaOH neutralise one mole of ethanedioic acid, $\text{HOOC-COOH}$?
How many water molecules are produced when one mole of a diol reacts with one mole of a dicarboxylic acid to form a single ester link?
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{1}$ — each ester link releases one water molecule.

Repeating that step many times over is **condensation polymerisation**, which is how polyesters are made.

questions.q: How many of these give a positive Tollens test: ethanal, propanone, methanal, ethanoic acid?
questions.solution:
**Ethanal** ✓ and **methanal** ✓ — both aldehydes.

**Propanone** ✗ (a ketone) and **ethanoic acid** ✗.

So $\mathbf{2}$. (Methanoic acid would be a third, since it contains a $-\text{CHO}$ group — but ethanoic acid does not.)

questions.q: Give the mechanism for the reaction of HCN with ethanal, explain the role of the base, and say why the product is racemic.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — generating the nucleophile.** A trace of base converts HCN into cyanide, a far better nucleophile:

$\text{HCN} + \text{OH}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{CN}^{-} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

**Step 2 — attack.** $\text{CN}^{-}$ attacks the $\delta+$ carbonyl carbon. The carbon changes from $sp^{2}$ to $sp^{3}$, and the $\pi$ electrons move onto the oxygen, giving an alkoxide.

**Step 3 — protonation.** The alkoxide takes a proton from HCN, giving the cyanohydrin and **regenerating** $\text{CN}^{-}$.

$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHO} + \text{HCN} \to \text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CN}$

**The base's role.** Pure HCN reacts extremely slowly; adding a trace of KCN or base speeds it up enormously, because the rate depends on $[\text{CN}^{-}]$ rather than on $[\text{HCN}]$.

That kinetic observation is the **evidence** for the mechanism: the attacking species is the ion, not the molecule.

**Why the product is racemic.** The planar carbonyl carbon can be attacked from **either face**, with equal probability, giving equal amounts of the two enantiomers.

The product contains a chiral centre — the carbon now carries H, OH, CN and $\text{CH}_{3}$ — but the mixture is optically inactive.

**Why cyanohydrins are useful.** The nitrile can be hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid or reduced to an amine, so this one step both **lengthens the carbon chain** and installs a new functional group.

**Safety:** HCN is extremely toxic, so the reaction is carried out in a fume cupboard using KCN with dilute acid rather than the gas itself.

questions.q: Describe how you would distinguish between propanal, propanone and propan-1-ol using chemical tests.
questions.solution:
**Test 1 — 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (Brady's reagent).**

**Propanal** ✓ and **propanone** ✓ give an **orange precipitate**; **propan-1-ol** gives nothing.

This separates the carbonyl compounds from the alcohol at one stroke. The precipitate's melting point, compared with tabulated values, even identifies **which** carbonyl compound it is.

**Test 2 — Tollens' reagent, warmed.**

**Propanal** gives a **silver mirror**; **propanone** does not.

This separates the aldehyde from the ketone, since only the aldehyde can be oxidised without breaking a C–C bond.

**Alternatively Fehling's solution:** a red-brown precipitate of $\text{Cu}_{2}\text{O}$ with the aldehyde only.

**Test 3 — acidified potassium dichromate, warmed.**

**Propanal** and **propan-1-ol** both turn it **orange to green**; **propanone** leaves it orange.

**A trap worth noting: the iodoform test would not help here.** Propanone gives it (it has a $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}-$ group), but so would ethanal — and neither propanal nor propan-1-ol does. It distinguishes the ketone but by an accident of structure rather than by class.

**A systematic scheme:** Brady's reagent first to find the carbonyls, then Tollens' to separate aldehyde from ketone. Two tests settle three compounds.

In an examination, always give the **reagent**, the **observation** and the **conclusion** — all three earn marks.

questions.q: Describe four reactions of carboxylic acids, explain esterification including how the yield is improved, and describe the hydrolysis of esters.
questions.solution:
**Four reactions.**

1. **With a carbonate:** brisk effervescence of $\text{CO}_{2}$.

$2\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH} + \text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3} \to 2\text{CH}_{3}\text{COONa} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \text{CO}_{2}$

This is the test that distinguishes a carboxylic acid from a phenol.

2. **With an alcohol:** esterification (below).

3. **With $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$:** reduction to a **primary alcohol**. $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ is not strong enough.

4. **With $\text{PCl}_{5}$:** an acyl chloride, plus misty fumes of HCl — itself a test for $-\text{OH}$.

**Esterification.**

$\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH} + \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_{3}\text{COOC}_{2}\text{H}_{5} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

Concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ catalyses it and, by absorbing water, also shifts the equilibrium right.

**Improving the yield:** remove the water as it forms, use an excess of the cheaper reagent, or distil the ester off — all applications of Le Chatelier's principle to a reversible reaction.

**Hydrolysis of esters — two routes.**

• **Acid hydrolysis** is simply esterification in reverse, and is therefore **reversible** and incomplete.

• **Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification)** gives the **carboxylate salt**, which cannot react back — so it goes to **completion**.

$\text{RCOOR}' + \text{NaOH} \to \text{RCOONa} + \text{R}'\text{OH}$

**This is how soap is made:** boiling animal or vegetable fat (an ester of glycerol) with sodium hydroxide gives the sodium salts of long-chain acids — soap — and glycerol as a valuable by-product.

questions.q: Explain why carboxylic acids are acidic, why chloroethanoic acid is stronger than ethanoic acid, and why phenol is weaker than both.
questions.solution:
**Why carboxylic acids are acidic.** On losing a proton, the carboxylate ion's negative charge is **delocalised over two equivalent oxygen atoms**.

The two resonance structures are identical, giving the maximum possible stabilisation, and X-ray measurements confirm that **both C–O bonds are the same length** — intermediate between a single and a double bond.

A stabilised conjugate base means a stronger acid.

**Why chloroethanoic acid is stronger.** Chlorine is electronegative and withdraws electron density **inductively** along the chain, spreading the carboxylate's charge still further and stabilising it more.

$\text{p}K_{a}$: ethanoic $4.76$, chloroethanoic $2.86$, dichloroethanoic $1.29$, trichloroethanoic $0.65$.

**Each chlorine multiplies the acidity roughly a hundredfold**, and the effect falls off sharply with distance — a chlorine three carbons away barely registers.

**Why phenol is weaker.** Phenoxide's charge is delocalised too, but onto **carbon** atoms of the ring, which hold a negative charge far less willingly than oxygen does.

Those resonance structures also disrupt the aromatic sextet, which costs energy. So the stabilisation is real but much weaker: $\text{p}K_{a}$ about $10$.

**The order, with the reason in one line each:**

carboxylic acid ($4.8$, charge on two oxygens) $>$ phenol ($10$, charge on carbons) $>$ alcohol ($16$, no delocalisation at all).

**The practical test that separates them:** only the carboxylic acid is strong enough to displace $\text{CO}_{2}$ from a carbonate.

questions.q: Describe the physical properties and uses of esters, and explain why they smell pleasant while carboxylic acids do not.
questions.solution:
**Physical properties.** Esters are **volatile liquids** with characteristically sweet, fruity smells, only slightly soluble in water but good solvents for organic compounds.

**Why they are volatile.** An ester has no O–H bond, so it **cannot hydrogen bond to itself**. Only dipole-dipole and dispersion forces hold the molecules together.

**Contrast the carboxylic acid it came from.** Acids hydrogen bond strongly and in fact form **dimers**, two molecules locked together by a pair of hydrogen bonds. They are far less volatile and boil much higher.

Ethyl ethanoate ($M_{r}$ $88$) boils at $77$°C; ethanoic acid ($M_{r}$ only $60$) boils at $118$°C.

**Why esters smell and acids do not smell pleasant.** To be smelled, a molecule must reach the nose — so volatility is essential. Esters evaporate readily and reach the receptors.

Carboxylic acids are less volatile, and what does reach the nose smells sharp and unpleasant: ethanoic acid is vinegar, butanoic acid is rancid butter, and the acids in goats and in sweat are the same compounds.

**Uses.**

• **Flavourings and perfumes** — pentyl ethanoate is pear drops, octyl ethanoate orange, ethyl butanoate pineapple. Natural fruit flavours are mostly ester mixtures.

• **Solvents** — ethyl ethanoate in nail varnish remover, glues and printing inks.

• **Plasticisers**, softening PVC.

• **Fats and oils** are esters of glycerol, and **biodiesel** is made by transesterifying them with methanol.

• **Polyesters** such as Terylene, from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid.
